title: Deploy the Beacon Catalog Service
scenario: A teammate has left a low-cost embedded beacon gateway half-deployed: it turns capture files into a queryable catalog, but the daemon gives inconsistent answers after reloads and on larger captures. The container contains a multi-stage Rust pipeline, a small opaque frame-decoder utility, capture data, deployment scripts, and a line-oriented TCP protocol that downstream firmware already speaks.
instruction_draft: Can you get the beacon catalog online at `/opt/beacon/bin/beacond`, listening on TCP port `4711`, and make it reliable without adding network dependencies? It must read captures from `/opt/beacon/data`, rebuild its snapshot with `/opt/beacon/bin/catalog-build`, and answer newline-delimited JSON requests: `{"op":"lookup","device":"<16 hex chars>","at":<integer>}`, `{"op":"history","device":"<16 hex chars>","from":<integer>,"to":<integer>}`, `{"op":"stats"}`, and `{"op":"reload"}`; preserve the response schemas documented in `/opt/beacon/PROTOCOL.md`, including ordering, quality, source sequence, and missing-device behavior. Please make reload atomic and consistent across all request types, keep the service bounded to the supplied 2 GB machine, and verify it against the supplied captures plus fresh capture directories generated by `/opt/beacon/tools/make_case.py`.
requirements: The service must listen on TCP port `4711`.
The service must read capture inputs from `/opt/beacon/data`.
The service must accept newline-delimited JSON over TCP.
The service must support lookup requests with fields `op`, `device`, and integer `at`.
The service must support history requests with fields `op`, `device`, integer `from`, and integer `to`.
Responses must follow the schemas in `/opt/beacon/PROTOCOL.md`.
Lookup responses must preserve the documented device, value, quality, and source-sequence fields.
History responses must preserve the documented ordering and record fields.
Missing devices and out-of-range timestamps must produce the documented non-success response rather than fabricated data.
Reload must atomically expose one internally consistent snapshot to all request types.
The service must work with the supplied captures and fresh cases generated by `/opt/beacon/tools/make_case.py`.
The solution must run within the container without network access or additional downloaded dependencies.
environment: The Dockerfile is based on `python:3.13-slim-bookworm`, installs pinned Rust/build/runtime packages, and creates `/opt/beacon`.
The repository contains roughly 1,700 lines across Rust crates for capture ingestion, snapshot building, the TCP daemon, and deployment helpers, plus Python case-generation tools and tests.

Capture inputs are split across many `.cap` files in `/opt/beacon/data`; files contain binary beacon frames with interleaved devices, sequence-number rollover, duplicate observations, corrupt padding, and timestamps that are not globally sorted.

`/opt/beacon/bin/frame-decoder` is a compiled opaque utility with no source shipped. It converts the documented capture-frame representation into canonical observation records and has behavior that must be learned from its command-line interface and experiments.
`/opt/beacon/bin/catalog-build` consumes decoder output and writes a snapshot plus a statistics sidecar under the configured state directory.
`/opt/beacon/PROTOCOL.md` documents the JSON request and response schemas, error forms, timestamp inclusivity, tie-breaking rules, and history ordering.

The initial deployment scripts contain plausible configuration, process-supervision, and reload logic, but the running components disagree on snapshot generation, sequence ordering, and replacement of the snapshot and statistics sidecar.
The supplied corpus is small enough to inspect manually but does not contain every rollover, duplicate, and cross-file ordering combination produced by the case generator.

`/opt/beacon/tools/make_case.py` deterministically creates fresh capture directories from a supplied seed, including thousands of observations, rare sequence wrap cases, duplicate timestamps, corrupt frames, and devices that disappear between generations.
internal_hint: First inspect the deployment entrypoint, protocol document, capture-build logs, and the opaque decoder's help/output rather than assuming the Rust reader is authoritative. Run the supplied daemon against the corpus while issuing all four protocol operations, then generate several seeded cases and compare decoder output, builder output, sidecar statistics, and daemon replies; the important failures only appear after enough records accumulate and when sequence numbers wrap or equal timestamps are duplicated. The durable fix is to make every stage consume the decoder's canonical record semantics, define one deterministic per-device ordering and deduplication rule for both snapshot and history, and publish the snapshot and sidecar through one generation directory followed by an atomic directory swap. The daemon must hold one immutable generation for each request and switch generations only between requests, so lookup, history, and stats cannot observe different builds. The reference solution is a deterministic shell script that inventories files, exercises the black-box decoder and protocol, generates multiple cases, patches the Rust/configuration components, rebuilds, and runs protocol-level checks.
trap: A shallow solution can make the supplied sample look correct by sorting only on timestamp, rebuilding the main snapshot without the sidecar, or locking only the reload handler. Hidden cases contain equal timestamps, sequence-number wraparound, duplicate records split across files, and requests racing a reload; such a solution returns a plausible but wrong source sequence, unstable history order, stale stats, or a mixture of two generations.
tests: The verifier starts the deployed service and checks that TCP port `4711` accepts newline-delimited JSON requests, corresponding to the instruction sentence requiring `/opt/beacon/bin/beacond` on TCP port `4711`.

It sends lookup requests for known, missing, boundary, and out-of-range devices/timestamps and compares exact response fields and error forms with the reference, corresponding to the instruction sentence requiring lookup requests and documented missing-device behavior.

It sends history requests over intervals with inclusive boundaries, equal timestamps, duplicate observations, and sequence rollover, then compares complete ordered records with the reference, corresponding to the instruction sentence requiring history requests and documented ordering.

It checks `stats` before and after building cases, including record counts, device counts, rejected-frame counts, and generation identifiers, corresponding to the instruction sentence requiring the documented response schemas.

It performs reloads while issuing concurrent lookup, history, and stats requests and rejects any response whose generation mixes snapshot data and sidecar metadata, corresponding to the instruction sentence requiring atomic and internally consistent reloads.

It runs `/opt/beacon/tools/make_case.py` with several hidden deterministic seeds, replaces the capture directory, rebuilds/reloads, and compares all protocol responses against a separately executed reference pipeline, corresponding to the instruction sentence requiring fresh generated capture directories.

It includes thousands of records, interleaved capture files, corrupt padding, duplicate timestamps, device disappearance, and 32-bit source-sequence rollover in verify-time cases, checking that the implementation generalizes beyond the supplied corpus.

It checks that the service survives malformed JSON, incomplete requests, unknown operations, and multiple requests on one connection according to `PROTOCOL.md`, corresponding to the instruction sentence requiring the documented JSON protocol.

It runs the deployment without internet access and monitors resource use while processing the largest generated case, corresponding to the instruction sentences forbidding downloaded dependencies and requiring operation within the supplied machine.

verifier_knob.name: request_scenarios
verifier_knob.value: 9 protocol scenario families across 6 hidden generated seeds, including reload races
verifier_knob.effect: Lowering this to the supplied corpus and a few sequential lookups lets timestamp-only or non-atomic implementations pass. Raising it adds more generated seeds, histories spanning rollover, malformed requests, and concurrent reload interleavings, increasing the chance that partial pipeline fixes and stale-sidecar deployments fail.

expected_failure_modes: The agent reads only the visible Rust daemon and misses the opaque decoder's canonicalization rules.
The agent validates one supplied capture and assumes timestamps are globally ordered or unique.
The agent uses signed or ordinary integer sequence comparisons across source-sequence rollover.
The agent deduplicates in the snapshot builder but not in history queries, or applies different tie-breaking rules in the two paths.
The agent updates the snapshot and statistics sidecar in separate filesystem operations, allowing mixed-generation responses.
The agent holds a reload lock but lets existing requests read mutable shared state while the generation is being replaced.
The agent hard-codes the supplied devices or records instead of implementing the capture pipeline for generated cases.
The agent returns syntactically valid JSON with the wrong field types, ordering, boundary semantics, or error response.
The agent adds an external crate or runtime service despite the offline deployment requirement.
The agent verifies only sequential lookup requests and never exercises history, stats, malformed input, or reload concurrency.
